extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in the history of the Catskills, Jewish American culture, and comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts style and cultural features of the Borscht Belt (Catskills) resorts and its comedic tradition — what defined the region's resorts, bungalow colonies, and the characteristic features/themes of Borscht Belt humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borscht Belt humor characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Borscht Belt humor refers to the rapid-fire, often self-deprecating style common to many of these performers and writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical elements and practice include quick delivery, self-deprecation, and reliance on concise one-liners and punchlines. The article gives example jokes and performers (Henny Youngman, Rodney Dangerfield, Don Rickles, etc.) to illustrate the mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical thematic content of Borscht Belt jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical themes include: Bad luck; Puns; Physical complaints and ailments (often relating to bowels and cramping); Aggravating relatives and nagging wives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists representative joke examples under each theme (e.g., Henny Youngman: 'I told the doctor I broke my leg in two places...'; Rodney Dangerfield's self-deprecating health/appearance lines; classic 'Take my wife—please!' style one-liners). These themes function as defining content tropes for the style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional comedic structure (set-up/punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Borscht Belt comedians typically took a traditional approach, with performers doing 'typical set up, punch lines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts this with modern 'podcast comics' who use more personal, longform approaches; use of tight set-up/punchline structure is presented as a criterion that distinguishes classic Borscht Belt style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resorts' accommodation of religious needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many larger hotels provided 'Friday night and holiday services as well as kosher cooking', supporting religious families to take vacations in accordance with their customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This facility (kosher cuisine and religious services) is presented as an important feature and selling point of Borscht Belt resorts, enabling observant Jewish families to vacation while maintaining religious practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bungalow colony layout and amenities
rubrics_metrics.description: Bungalows usually included 'a kitchen/living room/dinette, one bedroom, and a screened porch' with entertainment at the communal center (called the casino) being simple: bingo or a movie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuchaleyns (self-catered boarding houses) are described as having many small kitchens side-by-side and serving lower middle-class and working-class Jewish New Yorkers. These physical/layout features and modest communal entertainment types are part of what defined the bungalow colony experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on abundant food as a resort feature
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient choice of Jewish cuisine was an important feature of the hotels in the Borscht Belt, and 'too much was not enough' developed as a notion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jonathan Sarna is quoted explaining the cultural and historical reasons (immigrants' memories of hunger) for this emphasis; the abundance and centrality of food is treated as a defining hospitality standard of the resorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borscht Belt Historical Marker Project marker standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Markers are vertical interpretive highway markers enhanced with QR pegs for more in-depth explanations; they are double-sided with representative images and carry interpretive text about the specific area on one side and a common text about the Borscht Belt on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The project intends to place 20 markers strategically sited, include QR-enabled deeper content, and develop a self-guided audio tour system. The page reproduces the 'common text' that markers carry and lists placement/rollout plans and funding (Jewish American Society for Historic Preservation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hotels' use of entertainment/marketing to attract guests (singles scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hotels hired young male college students to attract single girls of a similar age; the singles scene was important and the Catskills 'became one great marriage broker.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hiring practice and the resulting singles-focused entertainment are presented as deliberate resort strategies to shape guest demographics and social life — a normative marketing/entertainment standard used by operators.
